title: Product Fragmenting Under Growth
excerpt: Product fragmentation under growth occurs when locally reasonable additions accumulate into inconsistent product logic. The result is a product whose parts differ in interaction model, terminology, assumptions, and governance.

bodyMarkdown:
## Product fragmentation under growth as a structural situation

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Product fragmentation under growth occurs when products grow by addition rather than design. Each addition may be locally reasonable: a filter for a market, a feature for a user type, a workflow change for a segment, or a module for a new capability. The aggregate can become a product whose sections no longer share coherent logic.

A fragmented product may use different interaction models, different terminology, and different assumptions about what users know or intend to do. Users experience the product as harder to use, even when they cannot identify a single broken feature.

The condition often remains invisible inside the product team because it accumulates incrementally. Each release is evaluated against the part of the product it changes, not against the whole product architecture. No single release creates the full problem, and no single team necessarily owns the resulting fragmentation.

## Why product fragmentation persists during growth

Product fragmentation persists when product governance is better at adding than at maintaining coherence. Three structural conditions allow fragmentation to accumulate without triggering intervention.

### No decommissioning discipline leaves legacy patterns in place

No decommissioning discipline means that superseded flows, features, and interaction patterns remain in the product after new versions are added. Removing the legacy version requires coordination across teams, product owners, market stakeholders, and support functions, and that coordination often does not assemble for removal alone.

The result is a product with multiple ways to perform the same task. These alternatives may not behave identically. Users form inconsistent mental models, and support queues receive questions the team no longer expects because the team has moved on from the old pattern while users still encounter it.

### Local optimisation without a global reference weakens product coherence

Local optimisation becomes a fragmentation mechanism when country teams, business unit teams, or feature teams optimise for their own scope without a shared architecture. A filter for Polish automotive buyers may be appropriate for that market. A workflow adapted for a media agency may be appropriate for that segment. The issue is not the local adaptation in isolation.

The issue is that no team is responsible for determining whether the sum of local optimisations still forms a coherent whole. Without a shared architecture that defines what is fixed and what may vary, each local optimisation becomes an ungoverned exception to product coherence.

### Governance for addition can outpace governance for coherence

Most products have operating mechanisms for addition: product management, roadmaps, sprint planning, and release cycles. Fewer products have equivalent mechanisms for assessing whether accumulated additions still form a coherent product.

A product grows into fragmentation when adding is the default activity and assessing coherence is not. In that condition, the governance structure of growth is stronger than the governance structure of product architecture.

## Costs across user experience, engineering, and organisation

Product fragmentation creates costs across three layers at the same time: user experience, engineering, and organisational coordination.

### User experience cost appears as difficulty without an obvious defect

Users who move between sections of a fragmented product encounter friction that feels like difficulty but is not always attributable to a single feature fault. The product no longer communicates its own logic reliably.

Support requests may rise because users cannot predict how one section will behave from experience in another section. Long-tenured users cope by memorising idiosyncrasies. New users take longer than they should to reach basic competence.

### Engineering cost appears as late-cycle rework and harder extension

Engineering teams working inside a fragmented product must navigate existing inconsistency before adding new functionality. Assumptions that hold in one product area may fail in another.

Rework can happen late in development cycles when cross-area inconsistency makes a seemingly simple change unexpectedly complex. The product becomes harder to extend with each release, even when the business case for extension is increasing.

### Organisational cost appears as weak alignment around what the product is

Teams that cannot coordinate on what the product should keep consistent cannot coordinate reliably on what to build next. Product managers cannot make reliable commitments about cross-team features when the behavioural baseline is unclear.

Marketing coordination can also be affected. Cross-market or cross-segment campaigns become harder when the same journey behaves differently in different contexts. The fragmented product exposes fragmented organisational alignment.

## OLX automotive marketplace as multi-market flow accumulation

OLX operates one of the largest classified advertising platforms in Central and Eastern Europe. In the automotive vertical, national markets including Poland, Portugal, Romania, and neighbouring countries had introduced their own filters, flows, and entry points for buyer and seller journeys.

The local adaptations responded to genuine market needs. Polish buyers use detailed technical filters. Trust signal patterns differ by market. The prevalence of in-app chat versus immediate phone contact varies across Central and Eastern Europe. The fragmentation did not come from individual decisions being wrong in isolation.

The aggregate created a platform that behaved differently by country in ways that made it increasingly difficult to steer. Product teams encountered feature bloat. Country managers continued pushing for local variations. Development reworked flows late in the cycle as cross-market inconsistencies surfaced during build. Marketing could not run cross-market campaigns reliably because the same journey behaved differently depending on where it was executed.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the OLX situation through Concept Convergence. Creative Navy produced a marketplace coherence framework that distinguished which journeys needed to remain consistent across markets from which points could allow country-level adaptation.

The OLX engagement produced delivery facts and structural outcomes. Country teams could propose adaptations within defined limits. Engineering had a stable reference. Marketing could plan cross-market campaigns against a known behavioural baseline. No user performance metrics were measured in the engagement. The competitive protection claim is inferred: the architecture creates structural conditions for resisting fragmentation, but whether those conditions have been tested under sustained growth is not independently confirmed.

## Pixelart Fugo as architecture that could not absorb new domains

Pixelart Fugo's digital signage CMS had a working product with a known NPS of 57%. The fragmentation problem was architectural rather than surface-level. The existing navigation structure could not accommodate new feature domains without disrupting what was already there.

Adding a capability required rethinking the architecture each time. The product had been built for its original scope and then grown beyond that scope without a structure that could absorb future growth.

Creative Navy's design work established two structural changes. The first was an extendable domain structure where new feature domains can be added without disrupting existing navigation. The second was an interlinking paradigm where content management, screen management, scheduling, and media creation can reference each other instead of operating as siloed modules.

The Pixelart Fugo outcomes are evidence-calibrated. NPS moved from 57% to 89%; this was client-measured before and after, with the second measurement approximately two months after launch, and was not independently verified. Revenue doubled in the two years following launch; this was client-reported, and the redesign was part of a broader growth phase that also included rebranding and commercial activity.

## IDEXX Animana as eleven years of accumulated workflow assumptions

Animana is one of the oldest veterinary practice management platforms in Europe. Eleven years of feature additions, local customisations, and workflow assumptions had accumulated into a fragmented platform.

The navigation was fragmented between consultation screens, lab results, and patient history. Multi-pet households required multiple windows to manage. Documentation flows interrupted consultations by requiring repeated section-switching. Clinical staff and receptionists were working around the interface with handwritten checklists near terminals and printed reference sheets taped to monitors.

Creative Navy-recorded field research across 35 clinics, 150+ participants, and 3 countries documented fragmentation at the level of observed behaviour. Receptionists had coping strategies for managing multiple animals per client at a glance. Clinical staff had strategies for avoiding interface clutter that came from reception-oriented layouts on consultation screens.

The engagement produced a 5-year product vision with 100+ development recommendations structured for direct translation into tickets. The primary architectural recommendation was separation of reception and clinical interfaces, reached through tension-driven reasoning across the research evidence. Client-reported evidence six months after the engagement indicates that the recommendations were well grounded and that some had already been implemented.

## Maritime traffic monitoring as portfolio fragmentation across separate teams

An engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators is a strong example of product fragmentation under growth. The portfolio covered nine products across four families: Vessel Traffic Services, River Information Services, a Voice Communication System, and an Integrated Communication System.

The interfaces had been designed by the software engineers who built them, in separate teams, and extended per customer contract and tender requirement over many years. The client had made individual improvements but had not commissioned a UX programme across the portfolio.

The engagement record identifies three commercial problems produced by fragmentation. Demonstrations did not communicate that the applications belonged to one family, even where the underlying systems exchanged information. Competing suppliers presented more coherent software during tender evaluation. Engineering teams rebuilt interface elements for each product and each customer project, creating repeated work, inconsistent behaviour, and maintenance cost.

This engagement must not be read as a nine-product redesign. Nine products were audited. One product was designed to full depth. Four received bounded transfer probes. Two received constraint and applicability reviews only. No commercial, tender, or engineering-efficiency outcome is recorded.

## Assemblio as product derivation and features from different eras

Assemblio GmbH shows product fragmentation at a smaller scale, with Assemblio's own description and criticism of its product attached. The Smart Viewer had been built from the Composer's components and looked almost identical to it, while the two user groups had different requirements.

Assemblio's own account also identified three different renaming interactions inside the Composer for three entity types. Folders used double-click. Projects used a menu item opening a dedicated screen. Products used a modal. Assemblio's stated reason was that the features had been built at different points in time.

This example should not be framed as a Creative Navy audit finding. No time-saving, adoption, or commercial metric attaches to the Assemblio material.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses fragmentation

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For product fragmentation under growth, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the architectural level rather than the feature level. Sandbox Experiments maps the existing structure as it is actually used, not only as it was designed to be used. That mapping distinguishes surface fragmentation, such as different visual treatments of similar functions, from structural fragmentation, such as different underlying models in different parts of the same product.

Concept Convergence identifies the architectural decisions that govern what must be consistent and what may vary. In this situation, the output is not only a design that is coherent at delivery. It is a governance reference that helps the organisation evaluate future additions.

Organizational Integration transfers that reference to the teams that will continue making growth decisions after the engagement. A design system without documented reasoning can be misapplied as the product grows. A coherence framework without organisational understanding can be eroded by the next local optimisation.

## Evidence boundaries for this situation

The examples on this page use different evidence strengths. OLX provides delivery facts and a structural framework, but no user performance metrics were measured. Pixelart Fugo includes client-measured NPS movement and client-reported revenue movement, with the revenue change occurring during a broader growth phase. IDEXX Animana includes Creative Navy-recorded field research across clinics, participants, and countries, plus client-reported follow-up. The maritime traffic monitoring example records the scope of audit and design activity but no commercial, tender, or engineering-efficiency outcome. Assemblio is attributed to Assemblio's own product description and criticism, not to a Creative Navy audit finding.

The evidence supports product fragmentation under growth as a recurring structural situation. It does not support a universal claim that a specific intervention guarantees user performance, revenue growth, competitive protection, or engineering-efficiency outcomes.

## Related pages

Product fragmentation under growth is closely related to situations where too many features reduce coherence, where new capabilities keep adding complexity, and where design debt turns into operational debt. It also overlaps with inconsistent product behaviour across scenarios and with stakeholder misalignment about product direction.
